extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of media studies, political economy, and critical/cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Describe and analyze Herman and Chomsky's five filters of the Propaganda Model — the structural criteria that, according to the model, shape mass media output under capitalism and produce an appearance of objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of the filters / appearance of objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: These filters allow the mass media to appear "objective" to audiences and discourage audiences from questioning the ways that the mass media uphold the ideological status quo and dominant groups/ideologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five filters are presented as structural mechanisms that collectively make media output seem neutral while aligning it with dominant interests; subsequent sections of the text discuss each filter in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 1: The size, concentrated ownership, owner wealth, and profit orientation of dominant media
rubrics_metrics.description: The size, concentrated ownership, owner wealth, and profit orientation of dominant media
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named as the first structural filter; implies that concentration of media ownership and owners' wealth/profit motives shape news selection and framing. (This page indicates a dedicated subsection 4.1.1 will discuss this filter in more detail.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 2: Advertising as the primary source of income for corporate media
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising as the primary source of income for corporate media
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the second structural filter: dependence on advertising revenue constrains media content and incentives. The page lists this filter as a key driver of media behavior; detailed discussion appears in subsequent sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 3: Reliance on "trusted sources" (government/business/corporate spokespeople)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reliance on "trusted sources," which frequently means using government or corporate spokespeople who spend vast sums on public relations and lobbying
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This filter emphasizes that media depend heavily on information from official, government, and corporate sources — actors who invest in PR and lobbying — thereby privileging elite viewpoints and restricting alternative voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 4: Disciplining the media through "flak"
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplining the media through "flak," both positive and negative
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the fourth filter; frames 'flak' (organized negative responses, pressure, or rewards) as a mechanism to police media content. The page identifies flak as both positive and negative forms of discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 5: "Anticommunism" (as a method of control; contemporary equivalents noted)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Anticommunism" a method of control (due to Manufacturing Consent being published during the final years of the Cold war; more current examples would be anti-socialism, anti-critical race theory, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally framed as anticommunism in the Cold War context, this fifth filter is presented as an ideological pretext that delegitimizes certain viewpoints; the text notes contemporary equivalents (e.g., anti-socialism, anti-critical race theory) that serve similar controlling functions.
